questions.question: The biological functions which perform gaseous exchange:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Photosynthesis     (b) Respiration     (c) Both a & b     (d) Growth
questions.explanation: Both photosynthesis (uses CO2, releases O2) and respiration (uses O2, releases CO2) involve exchange of gases between the organism and its environment.

questions.question: Plants do exchange of gases through:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Roots     (b) Stomata     (c) Stem     (d) All of these
questions.explanation: Plants exchange gases through stomata on leaves, lenticels on stems, and root hairs/root surface, so all listed structures are involved.

questions.question: Each stoma is formed by:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) one guard cell     (b) two guards cells     (c) three guard cells     (d) four guard cells
questions.explanation: A stoma (pore) is bordered by two bean-shaped guard cells whose swelling and shrinking opens and closes the pore.

questions.question: Respiratory surface possesses following property:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) thin and wet     (b) permeable     (c) very large     (d) all of these
questions.explanation: An efficient respiratory surface must be thin (short diffusion path), moist and permeable (for gases to dissolve and cross), and have a large surface area (for adequate exchange).

questions.question: Inspiration involves:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Contraction of intercostal muscles     (b) contraction of diaphragm     (c) Inward movement of ribs     (d) Both a & b
questions.explanation: During inspiration, both the external intercostal muscles and the diaphragm contract, enlarging the thoracic cavity and drawing air in; ribs move outward/upward, not inward.

questions.question: Larynx is located on:
questions.explanation: The larynx (voice box) sits at the top of the trachea, connecting the pharynx to the windpipe.

questions.question: The respiratory surface of human is:
questions.explanation: Gas exchange with blood actually occurs across the thin, moist walls of the alveoli, the tiny air sacs at the end of the bronchioles.

questions.question: Increase in rate of breathing is due to the following:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) increase CO2 in blood     (b) Increase O2 in blood     (c) decrease CO2 in blood     (d) decrease O2 in blood
questions.explanation: A rise in blood CO2 lowers blood pH, which is detected by chemoreceptors and stimulates the respiratory centre to increase breathing rate.

questions.question: Which of the following disorder is associated with degeneration of alveoli?
questions.explanation: Emphysema is characterized by breakdown and loss of elasticity of alveolar walls, reducing the surface area available for gas exchange.

questions.question: Which of the following disorder is associated with inflammation of air passage ways?
questions.explanation: Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchial tubes (air passages), often causing excess mucus production and coughing.

questions.question: Why the stomata generally open during day-time?
questions.answer: During daylight, photosynthesis occurs, so the plant needs to take in CO2 and release O2. Light also causes guard cells to accumulate potassium ions and water, becoming turgid and curving apart to open the pore. At night, without light, guard cells lose turgidity and the stomata close.

questions.question: Which parts of the plant intake CO2 and give out O2, and take in O2 and give out CO2 during day-time?
questions.answer: During the day, the green parts (mainly leaves, through stomata) take in CO2 and release O2 for photosynthesis. At the same time, every living cell of the plant, including roots, continuously takes in O2 and releases CO2 for respiration; during daylight the rate of photosynthesis usually exceeds respiration, so the net gas exchange is CO2 uptake and O2 release.

questions.question: Why do we have to breathe through nostrils rather than oral cavity?
questions.answer: Breathing through the nose is better because the nasal passages are lined with mucus and fine hair (cilia) that warm, moisten, and filter dust and microbes from incoming air before it reaches the lungs, protecting the delicate respiratory surfaces. The oral cavity lacks this filtering mechanism.

questions.question: Differentiate between breathing, gaseous exchange and respiration.
questions.answer: Breathing (ventilation) is the mechanical process of inhaling and exhaling air into and out of the lungs. Gaseous exchange is the diffusion of O2 from air into blood and CO2 from blood into air across the alveolar/respiratory surface. Respiration (cellular respiration) is the biochemical process inside cells in which glucose is broken down using O2 to release energy (ATP), producing CO2 and water as by-products.

questions.question: Why do we deep breathe during or immediately after exercise?
questions.answer: During exercise muscles respire faster and produce more CO2 while consuming more O2, sometimes building up an oxygen debt from anaerobic respiration. Deep breathing increases the volume of air exchanged, supplying more O2 and removing excess CO2/lactic acid by-products quickly to restore normal conditions.

questions.question: What is "oxygen debt"?
questions.answer: Oxygen debt is the extra amount of oxygen the body needs after strenuous exercise to break down the lactic acid that accumulated in muscles during anaerobic respiration (when oxygen supply was insufficient), converting it back to pyruvate/glucose or oxidising it completely.

questions.question: Distinguish between inspiration and expiration.
questions.answer: Inspiration is the act of drawing air into the lungs: the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, the thoracic cavity enlarges and air pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, so air rushes in. Expiration is breathing air out: the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax (or internal intercostals contract), the thoracic cavity shrinks, pressure inside rises above atmospheric pressure, and air is pushed out.

questions.question: What is lung cancer?
questions.answer: Lung cancer is the uncontrolled, abnormal growth of cells in the lung tissue, most commonly caused by long-term exposure to carcinogens such as those in tobacco smoke. It damages lung structure and function and can spread (metastasize) to other organs.

questions.question: How is asthma characterized?
questions.answer: Asthma is characterized by narrowing and inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles, often triggered by allergens, cold air, or exercise. It causes wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and coughing due to constriction of airway muscles and excess mucus secretion.

questions.question: Name five animals which use their body surface for gaseous exchange.
questions.answer: Earthworm, frog (through moist skin), leech, planaria (flatworm), and hydra are examples of animals that use their general body surface for gaseous exchange.

questions.question: What measures would you take to avoid respiratory disorders?
questions.answer: To protect the respiratory system one should: avoid smoking and second-hand smoke; avoid prolonged exposure to air pollution, dust, and industrial fumes (use masks where necessary); maintain good ventilation at home and work; avoid contact with people suffering from respiratory infections and practise good hygiene (covering mouth while coughing/sneezing, hand-washing); exercise regularly to keep lungs efficient; eat a balanced diet to support immunity; and get vaccinated against respiratory infections (e.g., influenza, pneumonia) and seek prompt medical treatment for infections such as bronchitis before they worsen.

questions.question: Discuss human respiratory system with the help of suitable illustrations.
questions.answer: Air enters through the nostrils into the nasal cavity, where it is warmed, moistened and filtered. It passes through the pharynx, then the larynx (voice box), into the trachea (windpipe) — a tube kept open by C-shaped cartilage rings. The trachea divides into two bronchi, one entering each lung, which further branch into smaller bronchioles ending in clusters of tiny air sacs called alveoli. Each alveolus is surrounded by a dense network of capillaries; its wall is one cell thick, providing a large, thin, moist surface for gas exchange. Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into the blood, while CO2 diffuses from blood into the alveoli to be exhaled. Breathing movements are driven by the diaphragm (a dome-shaped muscle below the lungs) and the intercostal muscles between the ribs, which alter the volume and pressure of the thoracic cavity to draw air in and push it out. (A labelled diagram should show: nostril → nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli, with the diaphragm at the base of the ribcage.)

questions.question: Prove with the help of an experiment that CO2 is released during respiration.
questions.answer: Take two conical flasks/test tubes, A and B. In flask A place some germinating seeds (or a small live animal such as a cockroach) on a platform above a small amount of KOH solution (to absorb any CO2 already present) inside the flask, and fit it with a delivery tube dipping into a test tube of freshly prepared lime water (Ca(OH)2 solution). Flask B is set up identically but is empty (no organism) or contains boiled/dead seeds, acting as a control. Leave both set-ups for some time. When air is drawn out or if the flask is closed and connected so exhaled gas passes through the lime water, the lime water in flask A (with living respiring seeds/organism) turns milky/cloudy, indicating the presence of CO2, because CO2 reacts with lime water to form insoluble calcium carbonate. The lime water in the control flask B remains clear. This proves that living, respiring organisms release CO2 as a product of respiration.

questions.question: Explain the process of ventilation in man.
questions.answer: Ventilation is the mechanical movement of air into and out of the lungs and has two phases: Inspiration — the diaphragm contracts and flattens downward while the external intercostal muscles contract, lifting the ribs upward and outward; this increases the volume of the thoracic cavity, lowering the air pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in through the nose/trachea into the lungs. Expiration — the diaphragm relaxes and arches upward while the intercostal muscles relax, decreasing the volume of the thoracic cavity; this raises the pressure inside the lungs above atmospheric pressure, forcing air out. This rhythmic cycle, controlled by the respiratory centre in the medulla oblongata of the brain, continuously renews air in the lungs to supply O2 and remove CO2.

questions.question: Why is smoking dangerous? How is it related to respiratory disorders?
questions.answer: Cigarette smoke contains harmful substances such as nicotine (addictive and raises blood pressure), tar (a carcinogen that coats and damages lung tissue), and carbon monoxide (reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood by binding haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen). Smoking paralyses and destroys the cilia lining the airways, so dust, microbes and mucus are not cleared, leading to bronchitis (inflammation of bronchi) and increasing infection risk. Tar deposits damage and can rupture alveolar walls, causing emphysema, and repeated cell damage caused by carcinogens can lead to uncontrolled cell division, causing lung cancer. Therefore, smoking is a major preventable cause of chronic bronchitis, emphysema and lung cancer.

questions.question: The internal condition of an organism is referred as:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Homeostasis     (b) Internal environment     (c) Internal metabolism     (d) Feedback mechanism
questions.explanation: The 'internal environment' refers to the conditions (temperature, water, ion concentration, etc.) inside the body/cells, which homeostasis acts to keep constant.

questions.question: A set of metabolic reactions which maintain internal environment is:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Positive feedback     (b) Negative feedback     (c) Osmoregulation     (d) Homeostasis
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is defined as the set of self-regulating processes that keep the internal environment of the body stable and constant.

questions.question: Removal of extra liquid water is:
questions.explanation: Guttation is the loss of excess liquid water in droplet form from the tips/edges of leaves, typically at night when transpiration is low but root pressure is high.

questions.question: Plants growing near coastal areas are called:
questions.explanation: Halophytes are plants adapted to grow in saline (salty) soils such as those found near coastlines.

questions.question: Organ of the human body considered the largest organ is:
questions.explanation: The skin, covering the entire external surface of the body, is the largest organ by surface area and weight.

questions.question: The maintenance of body temperature within suitable limits is called:
questions.explanation: Thermoregulation is the homeostatic process by which an organism keeps its body temperature within a narrow, functional range.

questions.question: The kidney is enclosed in a membrane called:
questions.explanation: The peritoneum lines the abdominal cavity and covers organs such as the kidneys; note the kidneys lie behind the peritoneum but are associated with it, unlike the pericardium (heart) or pleural membrane (lungs).

questions.question: The network of blood capillaries present in the layer of skin:
questions.explanation: The dermis, the middle layer of skin, contains blood capillaries, sweat glands, hair follicles and nerve endings; the epidermis is avascular.

questions.question: Selective reabsorption in the nephron takes place at:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Glomerulus     (b) Malpighian body     (c) Convoluted tubules     (d) Loop of Henle's
questions.explanation: Useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, salts and much water are selectively reabsorbed back into blood mainly at the proximal and distal convoluted tubules.

questions.question: The hormone ADH is released from:
questions.explanation: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is produced by the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary gland; it acts on the kidney tubules to increase water reabsorption.

questions.question: Why is homeostasis required?
questions.answer: Homeostasis is required to keep the internal conditions of the body (temperature, water balance, pH, ion concentration, glucose level, etc.) within narrow, stable limits, because enzymes and cell processes function properly only within a specific range; without homeostasis, cells and organs would malfunction and the organism could not survive changing external conditions.

questions.question: Why do plants remove liquid water instead of water vapour?
questions.answer: Guttation occurs when the soil is very moist and humidity is high (e.g., at night), so transpiration (loss of water vapour through stomata) is too slow to remove the excess water absorbed by roots under root pressure. In such conditions the excess water is pushed out in liquid form through special pores called hydathodes at leaf tips/margins instead of evaporating.

questions.question: How do plants survive in saltish water?
questions.answer: Halophytes (salt-tolerant plants) survive in saline water through adaptations such as: excreting excess salt through special salt glands in their leaves, storing salt in vacuoles of leaf cells to dilute it, having thick, fleshy (succulent) leaves that store water and dilute salt concentration, and possessing root membranes that restrict excessive salt uptake while allowing water absorption.

questions.question: Why is skin considered an excretory organ?
questions.answer: Skin is considered an excretory organ because sweat glands in the dermis secrete sweat, which contains water, salts (mainly sodium chloride) and small amounts of urea — a nitrogenous waste product — thereby removing metabolic wastes from the body along with helping in thermoregulation.

questions.question: What type of structures are present in dermis to perform different functions?
questions.answer: The dermis contains hair follicles, sweat glands, sebaceous (oil) glands, blood capillaries, sensory nerve endings (for touch, pressure, pain, temperature), arrector pili muscles, and connective tissue with collagen and elastic fibres, all of which contribute to protection, thermoregulation, excretion and sensation.

questions.question: Draw a neat and labelled diagram of nephron.
questions.answer: A nephron diagram should show: the Bowman's capsule surrounding a knot of capillaries called the glomerulus (together forming the Malpighian/renal corpuscle), leading into the proximal convoluted tubule, then the loop of Henle (descending and ascending limbs) dipping into the medulla, followed by the distal convoluted tubule, which opens into a collecting duct; blood vessels (afferent arteriole entering, efferent arteriole leaving the glomerulus, and a capillary network surrounding the tubules) should be labelled alongside each part.

questions.question: What is a kidney stone?
questions.answer: A kidney stone is a hard, crystalline deposit (commonly of calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate or uric acid) that forms in the kidney when minerals and salts in urine become too concentrated and crystallize, which can block the urinary tract and cause severe pain.

questions.question: How does human skin maintain temperature in cold conditions?
questions.answer: In cold conditions, blood vessels in the skin constrict (vasoconstriction) to reduce heat loss from the surface, the arrector pili muscles contract to raise hair and trap an insulating layer of air, and shivering (rapid involuntary muscle contraction) generates additional heat through increased metabolism, all helping to conserve body heat.

questions.question: When is dialysis required?
questions.answer: Dialysis is required when the kidneys fail to filter blood adequately (kidney/renal failure), so that waste products such as urea and excess salts and water accumulate in the blood to dangerous levels; an artificial kidney machine (dialysis) then filters the blood externally to remove these wastes and restore proper balance.

questions.question: Why is filtration at peritubular capillaries called ultra-filtration?
questions.answer: Filtration at the glomerulus (surrounded by peritubular/glomerular capillaries) is called ultra-filtration because blood is filtered under high pressure through a very fine filtering membrane, so that small molecules like water, glucose, salts and urea pass into the Bowman's capsule while blood cells and large protein molecules are held back — a much finer and more selective filtration than ordinary filtration.

questions.question: How does skin work as a thermoregulatory organ?
questions.answer: The skin regulates body temperature through several mechanisms. When the body is too hot: blood vessels in the dermis dilate (vasodilation), bringing more blood close to the skin surface so heat is lost by radiation; sweat glands secrete more sweat, which evaporates from the skin surface and cools the body; hair lies flat (arrector pili muscles relax), reducing the insulating layer of trapped air. When the body is too cold: blood vessels constrict (vasoconstriction) to reduce blood flow near the surface and minimise heat loss; sweat production decreases; arrector pili muscles contract, raising hairs to trap a layer of insulating air; and shivering (rapid involuntary contraction of skeletal muscles) generates extra heat. These responses are controlled by the hypothalamus, which acts as the body's thermostat, continuously monitoring blood temperature and triggering corrective mechanisms — a good example of negative feedback homeostasis.

questions.question: Describe the urinary system of man with the help of a diagram.
questions.answer: The human urinary system consists of a pair of bean-shaped kidneys located on either side of the vertebral column in the abdominal cavity, which filter blood and form urine. From each kidney, a ureter — a narrow muscular tube — carries urine down to the urinary bladder, a muscular sac that stores urine temporarily. From the bladder, urine passes out of the body through a single tube called the urethra during urination (micturition), controlled by sphincter muscles. (Diagram should show: two kidneys connected by ureters to a single urinary bladder, which opens to the exterior via the urethra, with renal artery and renal vein shown entering/leaving each kidney.)

questions.question: Describe the structure of the nephron within the L.S. of the kidney.
questions.answer: A longitudinal section of the kidney shows three main regions: the outer cortex, the inner medulla, and the pelvis (a funnel-shaped cavity that collects urine and leads into the ureter). Each kidney contains about a million functional units called nephrons. Each nephron begins with a Bowman's capsule (a cup-shaped structure) enclosing a tuft of capillaries, the glomerulus — together located in the cortex and forming the renal corpuscle, where blood filtration begins. This leads into a long, coiled proximal convoluted tubule (also in the cortex), which dips down into the medulla as the loop of Henle, then rises back into the cortex as the distal convoluted tubule. Several distal tubules join a collecting duct, which passes through the medulla and empties urine into the renal pelvis, and then into the ureter.

questions.question: Describe the network of blood vessels in the nephron and their functions.
questions.answer: Blood enters each nephron through an afferent arteriole, which branches into the glomerulus — a network of fine capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule — where high pressure forces water, glucose, salts, urea and other small molecules out of the blood into the capsule (ultra-filtration), while blood cells and large proteins are retained. The filtered blood leaves the glomerulus through a narrower efferent arteriole, which then branches into a second capillary network (peritubular capillaries) surrounding the proximal and distal convoluted tubules and the loop of Henle. These capillaries reabsorb useful substances (glucose, amino acids, salts, and most of the water) back into the blood from the tubule fluid, and also secrete additional wastes into the tubule (tubular secretion). Finally, these capillaries merge to form venules, which unite to form the renal vein, carrying purified blood away from the kidney.

questions.question: Describe different disorders of kidneys and their treatment.
questions.answer: Common kidney disorders include: Kidney stones — hard mineral deposits that form due to concentrated urine, causing pain and possible blockage; treated by increasing fluid intake to pass small stones, medication, or procedures like lithotripsy (shock-wave breaking of stones) or surgery for larger stones. Kidney (renal) failure — the kidneys lose the ability to filter blood adequately, due to causes such as diabetes, high blood pressure, or infection; treated with dialysis (haemodialysis using an artificial kidney machine, or peritoneal dialysis) to remove wastes from the blood, and in severe cases a kidney transplant. Nephritis — inflammation of the nephrons, often due to infection or autoimmune reaction, which can impair filtration; treated with medication (antibiotics/anti-inflammatory drugs), dietary control, and monitoring of kidney function. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) — bacterial infections of the urinary tract that can spread to the kidneys if untreated; treated with antibiotics and increased fluid intake.

questions.question: The activity in relation to changes in environment is:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Stimulus     (b) Response     (c) Both a & b     (d) None of these
questions.explanation: A stimulus is a detectable change in the environment, and the organism's activity to it is a response; the process together involves both.

questions.question: Stimulus is detected by:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Receptor     (b) Effector     (c) Nerve     (d) All of these
questions.explanation: Receptors are specialized cells/organs (e.g., sense organs) that detect stimuli and convert them into nerve impulses.

questions.question: The type of coordination through electrochemical signals is:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Nervous     (b) Chemical     (c) Mechanical     (d) All of these
questions.explanation: Nervous coordination works through electrochemical impulses transmitted along neurons.

questions.question: The chemicals released from one cell and carried to signal some distant cell through blood are:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Neurotransmitters     (b) Enzymes     (c) Hormones     (d) all of these
questions.explanation: Hormones are chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands into the blood, which carries them to target cells/organs elsewhere in the body.

questions.question: The type of coordination exhibited by plants:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Nervous coordination     (b) Chemical coordination     (c) Mechanical coordination     (d) Both a & d
questions.explanation: Plants lack a nervous system, so they coordinate their responses (growth, tropisms) using chemical messengers called plant hormones (e.g., auxins).

questions.question: The part of brain involved in reasoning is:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Fore brain     (b) Cerebrum     (c) Cortex     (d) Frontal lobe
questions.explanation: The cerebrum, the largest part of the forebrain, is responsible for higher mental functions including reasoning, memory, and intelligence.

questions.question: The part of brain involved in balance and precision in movements is:
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates muscle activity, maintains posture, and ensures balance and precision of voluntary movements.

questions.question: Vital functions for survival of animals are regulated by:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) CNS     (b) PNS     (c) somatic sub-division     (d) Autonomic sub-division
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system (a division of the PNS) controls involuntary vital functions such as heartbeat, breathing rate, and digestion.

questions.question: The shortest path of reflex action consists of:
questions.explanation: The simplest reflex arc (a monosynaptic reflex, e.g., knee-jerk) involves just a sensory neuron directly synapsing with a motor neuron — 2 neurons.

questions.question: The type of lens in our eye is:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Convex     (b) concave     (c) Both a & b     (d) None of these
questions.explanation: The eye lens is biconvex, allowing it to converge light rays onto the retina.

questions.question: The automatic process of altering focus to get a sharper image of a near object is:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Vision     (b) Accommodation     (c) Focus     (d) All of these
questions.explanation: Accommodation is the automatic change in the curvature/thickness of the eye lens (via ciliary muscles) to focus on objects at different distances.

questions.question: The vitamin necessary for proper vision is:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Vitamin A     (b) Vitamin B     (c) Vitamin C     (d) Vitamin D
questions.explanation: Vitamin A is required to make rhodopsin, the light-sensitive pigment in rod cells of the retina; its deficiency causes night blindness.

questions.question: A colour blind person cannot see:
questions.explanation: The most common form of colour blindness (red-green colour blindness) prevents a person from distinguishing red (and green) properly, due to defective cone cells.

questions.question: The book "Kitab-ul-Manazir" was written by:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Jabir bin Hayan     (b) Ibn-al-Haitham     (c) Ali Ibn-Isa     (d) Bu-Ali Sina
questions.explanation: Kitab-ul-Manazir (Book of Optics) was written by the Muslim scientist Ibn al-Haitham (Alhazen), a pioneer in the study of vision and light.

questions.question: Sensory hair-cells are present in:
questions.explanation: The cochlea of the inner ear contains rows of sensory hair cells that detect sound vibrations and convert them into nerve impulses.

questions.question: The gonads are the target organ for:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) FSH     (b) LH     (c) Both a & b     (d) None of these
questions.explanation: Both Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH) and Luteinizing Hormone (LH), secreted by the pituitary gland, act on the gonads (ovaries/testes) to regulate reproduction.

questions.question: What do you mean by feedback system?
questions.answer: A feedback system is a regulatory mechanism in which the output (result) of a process influences and controls further activity of that same process, so the body can maintain a stable internal state; in negative feedback (most common in homeostasis), a change triggers a response that reverses/reduces the change, restoring balance.

questions.question: Why is nervous coordination faster than chemical coordination?
questions.answer: Nervous coordination is faster because nerve impulses travel as rapid electrochemical signals along neurons directly to a specific target with almost instantaneous transmission, whereas chemical coordination relies on hormones diffusing into and being carried by the bloodstream, which is a much slower transport route reaching target organs less directly.

questions.question: Which of the two coordination types is better and why?
questions.answer: Neither is universally 'better' — they serve different needs. Nervous coordination is better for rapid, short-term, precise responses (e.g., reflexes), while chemical (hormonal) coordination is better for slower, longer-lasting, widespread effects (e.g., growth, metabolism, puberty). The body uses both together for complete, efficient control.

questions.question: How does reflex action work by a reflex-arc?
questions.answer: In a reflex arc, a receptor detects a stimulus and generates a nerve impulse, which travels along a sensory neuron to the spinal cord. There it may pass through a relay (connector) neuron and is transmitted to a motor neuron, which carries the impulse to an effector (muscle or gland), producing a rapid, automatic response — all without needing conscious involvement of the brain, which allows a very fast reaction to protect the body from harm.

questions.question: Why is a driving license not issued to a colour blind person?
questions.answer: A colour-blind person may be unable to correctly distinguish traffic light colours (red, amber, green) and other colour-coded road signs, which could lead to serious accidents; hence, for road safety, a driving license is not issued to such persons.

questions.question: Why does the thyroid gland swell up, and what is the name of the disease?
questions.answer: The thyroid gland swells up when it lacks sufficient iodine to produce thyroid hormone (thyroxine); to compensate, the gland enlarges in an attempt to trap more iodine and produce enough hormone. This condition is called goitre.

questions.question: What is the role of Islets of Langerhans cells?
questions.answer: The Islets of Langerhans are clusters of endocrine cells in the pancreas. Their beta cells secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose level by promoting its uptake and storage (as glycogen) in cells, while alpha cells secrete glucagon, which raises blood glucose by promoting the breakdown of glycogen into glucose, together regulating blood sugar homeostasis.

questions.question: What is "emergency hormone" and why is it named so?
questions.answer: Adrenaline (epinephrine), secreted by the adrenal glands, is called the 'emergency hormone' because it is rapidly released in stressful or dangerous ('fight or flight') situations, quickly increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and blood glucose level, and diverting blood to muscles to prepare the body for immediate physical action.

questions.question: What are the possible reasons of paralysis?
questions.answer: Paralysis can result from damage to the nervous system caused by: injury or trauma to the brain or spinal cord (e.g., accidents), stroke (interrupted blood supply to the brain), infections affecting nerves (e.g., polio), tumours pressing on nerves or the spinal cord, degenerative nerve diseases, or nerve damage from disease (e.g., multiple sclerosis).

questions.question: What is Epilepsy?
questions.answer: Epilepsy is a neurological disorder characterized by sudden, abnormal, excessive electrical activity in the brain, causing recurrent seizures that may involve convulsions, loss of consciousness, or unusual sensations/behaviour.

questions.question: Differentiate between Chemical and Nervous Coordination.
questions.answer: Nervous coordination uses electrochemical nerve impulses transmitted through neurons; it is fast-acting, short-lived, and produces a localized, precise response. Chemical coordination uses hormones secreted into the blood by endocrine glands; it is comparatively slow-acting, longer-lasting, and produces widespread effects on multiple target organs throughout the body.

questions.question: Discuss the detailed structure of the human brain.
questions.answer: The human brain is divided into three main regions: the forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain. The forebrain includes the cerebrum — the largest part, divided into two hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum, responsible for reasoning, memory, intelligence, voluntary movement, and interpretation of sensory information (organized into a sensory cortex, motor cortex, and association areas); and the thalamus and hypothalamus, which relay sensory information and regulate functions like temperature, hunger, thirst and hormone release. The midbrain relays visual and auditory information and helps control eye movement. The hindbrain includes the cerebellum, which coordinates balance, posture and precise voluntary movements, and the medulla oblongata and pons, which control vital involuntary functions such as heartbeat, breathing, and blood pressure, and connect the brain to the spinal cord. The entire brain is protected by the bony cranium, three membranes called meninges, and cushioned by cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.question: Write a note on the human eye or ear.
questions.answer: Human Eye: The eye is a spherical organ enclosed by three layers — the outer tough sclera (with the transparent cornea at the front for light entry), the middle pigmented choroid (with the iris controlling pupil size and the ciliary body controlling lens shape), and the inner light-sensitive retina containing rod cells (dim light, black-and-white vision) and cone cells (bright light, colour vision). Light entering through the cornea and pupil is focused by the lens onto the retina, where receptor cells convert light into nerve impulses carried by the optic nerve to the brain for interpretation. Human Ear: The ear has three regions — the outer ear (pinna and ear canal) collects sound waves and directs them to the eardrum (tympanic membrane), which vibrates; the middle ear contains three tiny bones (malleus, incus, stapes) that amplify these vibrations and transmit them to the oval window; the inner ear contains the fluid-filled, coiled cochlea, lined with sensory hair cells that convert vibrations into nerve impulses sent via the auditory nerve to the brain, allowing us to perceive sound. The inner ear also contains the semicircular canals, which help maintain balance.

questions.question: Why does the intelligence level of persons differ from each other, even though the components of the brain are the same?
questions.answer: Although all humans have the same basic brain structures (cerebrum, cerebellum, etc.), intelligence varies due to differences in genetic makeup (inherited traits affecting brain development and neural connections), the degree of development and density of neural connections (synapses) shaped by learning and experiences, environmental factors (nutrition, especially during early development, exposure to stimulating environments, education, and upbringing), and individual differences in how efficiently different brain regions process information. Together, genetic potential and environmental/experiential factors interact to determine each person's intelligence level.

questions.question: What is the endocrine system? Discuss the gland involved in regulation of blood glucose and how.
questions.answer: The endocrine system is a network of ductless glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream to regulate various body functions such as growth, metabolism, reproduction, and homeostasis, over a longer time-scale than the nervous system. The pancreas is the key gland regulating blood glucose level: its Islets of Langerhans contain beta cells, which secrete insulin when blood glucose rises (e.g., after a meal); insulin stimulates body cells (especially liver and muscle) to take up glucose from the blood and store it as glycogen, lowering blood glucose. Alpha cells secrete glucagon when blood glucose falls (e.g., during fasting); glucagon stimulates the liver to break down stored glycogen into glucose and release it into the blood, raising blood glucose level. Together, insulin and glucagon work through negative feedback to keep blood glucose within a normal, stable range.

questions.question: What is diabetes mellitus? Explain some ways of its management.
questions.answer: Diabetes mellitus is a metabolic disorder in which the body either does not produce enough insulin (Type 1 diabetes, usually due to autoimmune destruction of beta cells) or the body's cells do not respond properly to insulin (Type 2 diabetes, often linked to obesity/lifestyle), resulting in persistently high blood glucose levels. Management includes: regular monitoring of blood glucose levels; insulin injections (essential for Type 1, sometimes needed in Type 2); oral medications that help the body use insulin more effectively or reduce glucose production (mainly for Type 2); maintaining a controlled, balanced diet low in refined sugars; regular physical exercise to help control blood glucose and maintain healthy weight; and regular medical check-ups to prevent/manage complications affecting the eyes, kidneys, nerves, and heart.

questions.question: Irritation caused by stimulus is the main cause of:
questions.explanation: Movement (the response of an organism/part of it to a stimulus) is caused by irritability — the ability to detect and respond to a stimulus.

questions.question: The framework which gives shape to any structure is called:
questions.explanation: The skeleton is the supporting framework of the body that gives it shape and structure.

questions.question: The cartilage is made up of cells called:
questions.explanation: Chondrocytes are the living cells embedded in the matrix of cartilage tissue.

questions.question: The head of femur is attached with:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Pelvic girdle     (b) Pectoral girdle     (c) Scapula     (d) Acetabulum of pelvic girdle
questions.explanation: The rounded head of the femur fits into the acetabulum, a cup-shaped socket in the pelvic girdle, forming the hip (ball-and-socket) joint.

questions.question: The large muscle of the arm is:
questions.explanation: The triceps is actually the larger muscle on the back of the upper arm (though biceps is often mistaken as larger, per this textbook's answer key the triceps is considered the larger arm muscle).

questions.question: The band of tough, fibrous, connective tissue which is attached to bone at joints is called:
questions.explanation: Ligaments are tough fibrous connective tissue bands that connect bone to bone at joints, providing stability.

questions.question: Softening and weakening of bone in children due to deficiency of vitamin D is called:
questions.explanation: Rickets is a childhood bone disorder caused by vitamin D deficiency, resulting in soft, weak, and deformed bones.

questions.question: The muscle which is responsible to straighten the limb is:
questions.explanation: Extensor muscles straighten (extend) a joint, while flexors bend (flex) it.

questions.question: The pair of muscles where both work in opposite directions is:
questions.explanation: Antagonistic muscle pairs (like biceps and triceps) work opposite to each other — one contracts while the other relaxes — to move a joint in two directions.

questions.question: What are the main functions of the skeleton?
questions.answer: The skeleton provides support and shape to the body, protects delicate internal organs (e.g., skull protects brain, rib cage protects heart/lungs), allows movement and locomotion by providing attachment points for muscles that act as levers, produces blood cells (in bone marrow), and stores minerals such as calcium and phosphorus.

questions.question: Distinguish between bone and cartilage.
questions.answer: Bone is a hard, rigid connective tissue with a matrix impregnated with calcium salts, containing living cells called osteocytes; it is well supplied with blood vessels and nerves. Cartilage is a softer, more flexible connective tissue with a matrix that is not calcified (mostly made of collagen and elastic fibres), containing cells called chondrocytes; it generally lacks a direct blood supply and is more elastic than bone.

questions.question: Locate the cartilages in different organs.
questions.answer: Cartilage is found at the tip of the nose (nasal cartilage), in the outer ear (pinna), in the walls of the larynx, trachea and bronchi (as supportive rings), at the ends of long bones and in joints (articular cartilage), between vertebrae (intervertebral discs), and forming the flexible parts of the rib cage connecting ribs to the sternum.

questions.question: Enlist the name and number of bones present in hind limb.
questions.answer: Each human hind limb (leg) contains: 1 femur (thigh bone), 1 patella (kneecap), 1 tibia and 1 fibula (lower leg), 7 tarsals (ankle bones), 5 metatarsals (foot bones), and 14 phalanges (toe bones) — a total of 30 bones in one leg.

questions.question: Locate the immovable joints in the human body.
questions.answer: Immovable (fixed/fibrous) joints are found in the skull, where the flat bones (cranial bones) are fused together at sutures, allowing no movement and providing strong protection to the brain.

questions.question: Draw a neat and labeled diagram of a hinge joint and a ball-and-socket joint.
questions.answer: A hinge joint diagram (e.g., the elbow or knee) should show two bones connected so movement occurs in only one plane, like a door hinge, with ligaments holding the bones together and cartilage cushioning the joint surfaces — labelled with bone names, ligament, and cartilage. A ball-and-socket joint diagram (e.g., the hip or shoulder) should show the rounded head ('ball') of one bone fitting into a cup-shaped cavity ('socket') of another bone, allowing movement in multiple directions/planes — labelled with the ball (e.g., femur head), socket (e.g., acetabulum), and surrounding ligaments.

questions.question: What is rickets? Give its causes.
questions.answer: Rickets is a bone disorder in children in which bones become soft, weak, and deformed (often bowed legs). It is mainly caused by a deficiency of vitamin D, which is needed for the absorption of calcium and phosphate from food; without enough vitamin D, bones fail to mineralize (harden) properly. Insufficient exposure to sunlight (needed for the body to synthesize vitamin D) and poor diet lacking calcium/vitamin D also contribute.

questions.question: Distinguish between ligament and tendon.
questions.answer: A ligament is a tough, fibrous connective tissue that connects bone to bone at a joint, providing stability and limiting excessive movement. A tendon is a tough, fibrous connective tissue that connects muscle to bone, transmitting the force of muscle contraction to move the bone.

questions.question: Locate the hinge joint in the human body.
questions.answer: Hinge joints are found at the elbow (between humerus and ulna), the knee (between femur and tibia), and the joints of the fingers and toes (phalanges), allowing movement in one plane only, like the opening and closing of a door.

questions.question: What do you mean by biceps and triceps muscles?
questions.answer: The biceps is a muscle on the front of the upper arm that contracts to bend (flex) the arm at the elbow, bringing the forearm toward the shoulder. The triceps is a muscle on the back of the upper arm that contracts to straighten (extend) the arm at the elbow. They work as an antagonistic pair — when one contracts, the other relaxes.

questions.question: Prove that the skeletal system is a dynamic system.
questions.answer: The skeletal system is dynamic (constantly active and changing) rather than a fixed, static framework, because: bone tissue is continuously remodelled throughout life — old bone matrix is broken down by cells called osteoclasts while new bone is deposited by osteoblasts, allowing bones to grow, repair after fractures, and adapt their strength in response to the stresses placed on them (e.g., bones thicken with exercise/weight-bearing activity). Bones also actively store and release minerals (calcium, phosphorus) to help maintain their homeostatic levels in the blood. Additionally, bone marrow inside bones is constantly producing new blood cells (red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets) throughout a person's life. Since it is metabolically active, capable of self-repair, mineral exchange, and blood cell production, the skeleton is correctly described as a dynamic, living system rather than an inert supporting structure.

questions.question: Describe the flexion and extension in the human arm.
questions.answer: Flexion and extension of the arm occur at the elbow joint (a hinge joint) through the antagonistic action of the biceps and triceps muscles. In flexion, the biceps muscle (on the front of the upper arm) contracts and shortens, while the triceps relaxes; this pulls the forearm bones (radius and ulna) upward, bending the arm at the elbow, decreasing the angle between the forearm and upper arm. In extension, the triceps muscle (on the back of the upper arm) contracts and shortens, while the biceps relaxes; this straightens the arm at the elbow, increasing the angle between forearm and upper arm back to a straight position. Both muscles are attached to the bones via tendons, and because one muscle of the pair always relaxes as the other contracts, smooth, controlled movement of the arm is achieved.

questions.question: Explain disorders of bones and their causes.
questions.answer: Common bone disorders include: Rickets — softening and deformity of bones in children due to vitamin D deficiency, which impairs calcium absorption needed for proper bone mineralization. Osteoporosis — bones become porous, brittle, and weak due to loss of bone density, often caused by ageing, calcium/vitamin D deficiency, hormonal changes (e.g., after menopause), or lack of physical activity, increasing the risk of fractures. Osteoarthritis — degeneration of the cartilage cushioning joints, causing pain, stiffness, and swelling, commonly caused by ageing, joint overuse, injury, or obesity. Fractures — breaks in bone caused by excessive mechanical force, trauma, or accidents, sometimes worsened by weakened bones (e.g., from osteoporosis). Rheumatic/Rheumatoid conditions — inflammation of joints, in rheumatoid arthritis caused by an autoimmune reaction where the body's immune system attacks joint tissue, causing pain, swelling, and joint damage.

questions.question: The process which is essential for continuation and survival of species is:
questions.explanation: Reproduction produces new individuals, ensuring the continuation and survival of a species across generations.

questions.question: The type of reproduction which is necessary for evolution is:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Vegetative propagation     (b) Fragmentation     (c) Sexual reproduction     (d) Cloning
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from two parents, producing genetic variation among offspring, which is the raw material required for evolution by natural selection.

questions.question: The unicellular structure, responsible for asexual reproduction without fusion, is:
questions.explanation: Spores are single-celled reproductive units that can develop into new individuals without the fusion of two gametes, characteristic of asexual reproduction.

questions.question: The example of a stem which runs horizontally on the surface of soil to produce vegetatively is:
questions.explanation: Mint reproduces vegetatively via a runner/stolon — a stem that grows horizontally along the soil surface and produces new plants at its nodes.

questions.question: Plant stems that arise from buds on the base of parent plants are:
questions.explanation: Suckers are shoots that arise from buds at the base of the stem or from underground roots of the parent plant, growing into new independent plants.

questions.question: The type of seed production without fusion of male and female gametes is:
questions.explanation: Apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction in plants where seeds are formed without fertilization (fusion of gametes).

questions.question: The female gametophyte of angiospermic plant is:
questions.explanation: The embryo sac, located inside the ovule, is the female gametophyte of a flowering plant, containing the egg cell and other nuclei.

questions.question: The 3N (triploid) zygote in angiosperm develops into:
questions.explanation: In angiosperms, double fertilization produces a triploid (3N) primary endosperm nucleus, which develops into the endosperm — the nutritive tissue for the developing embryo.

questions.question: The male gonads in rabbit are:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Testis     (b) Ovaries     (c) Scrotal sac     (d) Vas deferens
questions.explanation: Testes are the primary male reproductive organs (gonads) that produce sperm and male hormones; the scrotal sac merely houses the testes.

questions.question: The female gametes are fertilized in the:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Oviduct     (b) Fallopian tube     (c) Ovaries     (d) Both a and b
questions.explanation: The oviduct is also known as the Fallopian tube; fertilization of the egg by sperm normally occurs in the upper part of this tube.

questions.question: Distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction, Epigeal and Hypogeal Germination.
questions.answer: Asexual reproduction involves a single parent producing offspring genetically identical to itself, without fusion of gametes (e.g., budding, fragmentation, vegetative propagation). Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes from (usually) two parents, producing genetically varied offspring. Epigeal germination is a type of seed germination in which the cotyledons are pushed above the soil surface due to elongation of the hypocotyl (e.g., in bean/gram). Hypogeal germination is germination in which the cotyledons remain below the soil surface, while the epicotyl elongates and pushes the plumule upward (e.g., in pea/maize).

questions.question: Draw a neat and labeled diagram of T.S. of an Angiospermic flower.
questions.answer: A transverse section (T.S.) of a flower should show, from outermost to innermost whorl: the calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens, each with a filament and anther containing pollen sacs), and gynoecium/carpel (with stigma, style, and ovary containing ovules) — each part clearly labelled in the cross-sectional arrangement.

questions.question: How does a new plant develop with an already growing plant?
questions.answer: New plants can develop from an already growing plant through vegetative propagation, where a part of the parent plant (such as a stem cutting, root, leaf, runner, sucker, rhizome, tuber, or bulb) separates or is used to grow into a completely new, independent plant that is genetically identical to the parent, without involving seeds or fertilization.

questions.question: How do leaves develop into new plants?
questions.answer: In some plants, such as Bryophyllum, small buds form along the margins (notches) of the leaves. Each of these buds contains meristematic tissue and can develop roots and shoots of its own; when the leaf falls to the ground or is placed on soil, these buds grow into complete new independent plants — a form of vegetative propagation.

questions.question: Draw a neat and labelled diagram of an Ovule.
questions.answer: An ovule diagram should show: the funicle (stalk attaching ovule to placenta), the outer and inner integuments surrounding the nucellus, a small opening called the micropyle at one end, the chalaza (base where integuments meet), and inside the nucellus, the embryo sac containing the egg cell, synergids, polar nuclei, and antipodal cells — all labelled.

questions.question: Draw a neat and labelled diagram of the male gametophyte of an angiospermic plant.
questions.answer: The male gametophyte (pollen grain) diagram should show: the outer thick wall (exine) with pores, the inner thin wall (intine), and inside, the vegetative (tube) nucleus and the generative cell/nucleus, which later divides to form two male gametes — all clearly labelled.

questions.question: List out the male reproductive organs of rabbit with glands.
questions.answer: The male reproductive organs of a rabbit include: a pair of testes (enclosed in the scrotal sac) which produce sperm; the epididymis, which stores and matures sperm; the vas deferens, which carries sperm from the epididymis; and accessory glands — seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and Cowper's (bulbourethral) glands — which secrete fluids that nourish and help transport sperm, together forming semen; the urethra passes through the penis, the organ used to deliver sperm into the female reproductive tract.

questions.question: What are STDs?
questions.answer: STDs (Sexually Transmitted Diseases) are infections that spread primarily through sexual contact, caused by bacteria, viruses, or parasites; examples include gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydia, genital herpes, and HIV/AIDS. They can affect the reproductive system and overall health, and some can be prevented through safe practices and awareness.

questions.question: Why is population control considered important for a prosperous society?
questions.answer: Population control is important because a rapidly growing population puts excessive pressure on limited resources such as food, water, housing, healthcare, education, and employment opportunities. Uncontrolled population growth can lead to poverty, unemployment, overcrowding, environmental degradation, and strain on infrastructure and public services, hindering a country's economic development; controlling population growth helps ensure resources and opportunities are sufficient for a better standard of living, supporting a more prosperous and sustainable society.

questions.question: Draw the life cycle of an Angiospermic plant.
questions.answer: The life cycle diagram should show the sequence: a mature flower with anthers producing pollen grains (male gametophyte) and ovary containing ovules (with embryo sac/female gametophyte) → pollination (transfer of pollen to stigma) → pollen tube growth down the style → double fertilization in the ovule (fusion of one male gamete with egg forming a diploid zygote, and another male gamete with polar nuclei forming triploid endosperm) → ovule develops into a seed (zygote develops into embryo) and ovary develops into fruit → seed dispersal → germination of seed → growth into a new seedling → mature plant, completing the cycle back to flowering.

questions.question: Describe natural asexual reproduction in plants.
questions.answer: Natural asexual (vegetative) reproduction in plants occurs without the fusion of gametes, producing offspring identical to the parent, through modified plant parts such as: Roots — e.g., sweet potato roots can develop buds that grow into new plants. Stems — e.g., runners/stolons (mint, strawberry) that creep along the ground and root at nodes; rhizomes (ginger) that are underground stems producing new shoots; tubers (potato) with 'eyes' (buds) that sprout into new plants; bulbs (onion) with fleshy, food-storing leaf bases that can grow into new plants; and suckers (banana) arising from the base of the parent stem. Leaves — e.g., in Bryophyllum, buds along the leaf margin develop into new plantlets. This form of reproduction allows plants to multiply quickly and colonize an area without depending on pollination or seed formation.

questions.question: What is pollination? Give adaptive characters of wind and insect pollinated flowers.
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther (male part) of a flower to the stigma (female part) of the same or another flower, which is a necessary step before fertilization can occur. Wind-pollinated flowers typically have: small, dull-coloured petals (or no petals) since they don't need to attract insects; no nectar or scent; large amounts of light, smooth, dry pollen produced in huge quantities to compensate for pollen wasted in air; long, feathery or exposed stigmas to catch airborne pollen; and anthers often hanging loosely outside the flower to release pollen easily into air currents. Insect-pollinated flowers typically have: large, brightly coloured petals to attract insects; scent and nectar as a reward for pollinators; pollen grains that are often sticky or spiny so they cling to an insect's body; and a sticky stigma to trap pollen brought by visiting insects.

questions.question: Describe different types of asexual reproduction in animals.
questions.answer: Asexual reproduction in animals occurs by: Binary fission — a single parent organism (e.g., Amoeba, Paramecium) divides into two equal daughter individuals. Budding — a small outgrowth (bud) forms on the parent's body (e.g., Hydra), grows, and eventually detaches to become an independent new organism, or in some cases remains attached forming a colony. Fragmentation — the parent body breaks into fragments (e.g., Planaria, starfish), and each fragment is capable of regenerating into a complete new organism. Regeneration — closely related to fragmentation, where a lost or separated body part regrows into a new complete organism in simple animals with high regenerative capacity.

questions.question: Describe the process of spermatogenesis.
questions.answer: Spermatogenesis is the process of sperm formation that occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testes. It begins with diploid germinal cells called spermatogonia, which multiply by mitosis. Some spermatogonia grow in size to become primary spermatocytes (still diploid). Each primary spermatocyte undergoes the first meiotic division to form two haploid secondary spermatocytes. Each secondary spermatocyte then undergoes the second meiotic division, producing a total of four haploid spermatids from each primary spermatocyte. These spermatids then undergo a process called spermiogenesis, in which they differentiate — developing a head (with a nucleus and acrosome containing enzymes), a middle piece (packed with mitochondria for energy), and a tail (flagellum for motility) — transforming into mature, motile sperm cells capable of fertilizing an egg.

questions.question: What is germination? Give the conditions of germination and also describe the methods of different germination.
questions.answer: Germination is the process by which a dormant seed resumes growth and develops into a seedling under favourable conditions. Conditions required for germination include: adequate water/moisture (to soften the seed coat and activate enzymes), suitable temperature (for enzyme activity and metabolic processes), sufficient oxygen (for aerobic respiration to provide energy), and in some seeds, light (though many germinate in darkness, some require light or darkness specifically). Types of germination: Epigeal germination — the hypocotyl (region below the cotyledons) elongates rapidly, pushing the cotyledons above the soil surface where they may become green and photosynthesize temporarily (e.g., bean, castor, gram). Hypogeal germination — the hypocotyl remains short, so the cotyledons stay below the soil surface, while the epicotyl (region above the cotyledons) elongates, pushing the plumule (young shoot) up through the soil (e.g., pea, maize, gram in some cases).

questions.question: Branch of biology that deals with the study of heredity and variation is called:
questions.explanation: Genetics is the specific branch of biology devoted to studying heredity (how traits pass from parents to offspring) and variation among organisms.

questions.question: The way by which genes transmit characters from parents to offspring is:
questions.explanation: Inheritance refers to the actual transmission/passing of genetic characters from parents to offspring.

questions.question: Two similar chromosomes in a cell which are similar in shape, size and position of centromere are called:
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes are pairs (one from each parent) that match in size, shape, and centromere position, carrying genes for the same traits.

questions.question: The chemical material of a chromosome is called:
questions.explanation: Chromatin is the complex of DNA and proteins that makes up the chemical material of chromosomes.

questions.question: The outer part of the DNA helix made up of sugar and phosphate is called:
questions.explanation: The sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA is held together by phosphoester (phosphodiester) bonds, forming the outer 'rails' of the double helix.

questions.question: The small segment of DNA which has information to code one protein is called:
questions.explanation: A gene is the basic functional unit of heredity — a segment of DNA that carries the code for a specific protein or trait.

questions.question: The exact duplication of DNA is called:
questions.explanation: DNA replication is the process by which a DNA molecule makes an identical copy of itself before cell division.

questions.question: If both the parents donate the same factor(s) of a character, it is called:
questions.explanation: Homozygous refers to an individual having two identical alleles (from both parents) for a particular gene/trait.

questions.question: The genetic constitution of a trait is called:
questions.explanation: Genotype refers to the actual genetic makeup (allele combination) of an organism for a trait, as opposed to phenotype, which is its physical/observable expression.

questions.question: What is a gene and how does it work?
questions.answer: A gene is a segment of DNA located on a chromosome that carries the coded instructions (in the sequence of its bases) for producing a specific protein or determining a particular trait. It works by being transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA), which is then translated at ribosomes into a specific protein; this protein then performs a function in the cell that ultimately produces the observable trait.

questions.question: Define the following terms: (a) Homologous Chromosome (b) Heterologous Chromosome (c) Dominant allele (d) Allele (e) Recessive allele (f) Homozygous (g) Heterozygous
questions.answer: (a) Homologous Chromosome: A pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, matching in size, shape, and centromere position, carrying genes for the same traits at corresponding loci. (b) Heterologous Chromosome: Chromosomes that are not matching/paired — i.e., non-homologous chromosomes that differ in size, shape, and gene content. (c) Dominant allele: An allele that expresses its effect (phenotype) whenever present, even in the presence of a different (recessive) allele, masking the recessive allele's effect. (d) Allele: One of two or more alternative forms of a gene that occupy the same position (locus) on homologous chromosomes and control the same trait. (e) Recessive allele: An allele whose effect is masked/not expressed in the phenotype when a dominant allele is present; it is only expressed when present in the homozygous condition. (f) Homozygous: Having two identical alleles (both dominant or both recessive) for a particular gene. (g) Heterozygous: Having two different alleles (one dominant, one recessive) for a particular gene.

questions.question: Which of the phenomena of inheritance is there where both factors express in heterozygous condition?
questions.answer: This phenomenon is called co-dominance (closely related to incomplete dominance), in which both alleles of a gene are fully and simultaneously expressed in the heterozygous condition, rather than one masking the other or blending — for example, in the AB blood group where both A and B alleles are expressed together.

questions.question: List out the factors which are involved in the theory of natural selection.
questions.answer: The main factors involved in Darwin's theory of natural selection are: overproduction of offspring (organisms produce more offspring than can survive); variation among individuals of a species; struggle for existence/competition for limited resources (food, space, mates); survival of the fittest (individuals with favourable variations are more likely to survive and reproduce); and inheritance of favourable variations to the next generation, gradually leading to evolutionary change over many generations.

questions.question: Relate artificial selection with natural selection.
questions.answer: In natural selection, nature/the environment acts as the selective force, allowing organisms best adapted to their environment to survive and reproduce, passing on favourable traits over many generations without human intervention. In artificial selection, humans (breeders) deliberately choose organisms with desirable traits (e.g., higher milk yield, disease resistance) to breed, intentionally guiding which traits are passed on. Both processes work on the same underlying principle — selecting individuals with particular heritable variations to reproduce more, gradually changing the characteristics of a population over generations — but natural selection is driven by environmental pressures, while artificial selection is driven by human choice.

questions.question: Describe the Watson and Crick model of DNA.
questions.answer: In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix model of DNA structure. According to this model, DNA consists of two long polynucleotide chains (strands) that are twisted around each other to form a double helix, resembling a twisted ladder. Each strand is made of a sugar (deoxyribose)-phosphate backbone on the outside, forming the 'side rails' of the ladder, connected by phosphoester bonds. The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between pairs of nitrogenous bases projecting inward, forming the 'rungs' of the ladder: Adenine (A) always pairs with Thymine (T) via two hydrogen bonds, and Guanine (G) always pairs with Cytosine (C) via three hydrogen bonds — this is called complementary base pairing. The two strands run in opposite (antiparallel) directions. This structure explained how DNA can store genetic information in the sequence of its bases and how it can be accurately copied (replicated), since each strand can serve as a template for making a new complementary strand.

questions.question: How does gene expression work? Describe in detail.
questions.answer: Gene expression is the process by which the information encoded in a gene (DNA) is used to produce a functional product, usually a protein, through two main steps: Transcription — the DNA double helix unwinds at the gene's location, and one strand acts as a template; the enzyme RNA polymerase reads this template strand and synthesizes a complementary single strand of messenger RNA (mRNA), copying the genetic code from DNA (with uracil replacing thymine). Translation — the mRNA moves from the nucleus to a ribosome in the cytoplasm, where it is 'read' three bases (a codon) at a time; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules bring specific amino acids that match each codon (via their anticodon), and the ribosome links these amino acids together in the correct sequence, forming a polypeptide chain. This polypeptide then folds into a functional protein, which carries out a specific role in the cell, ultimately producing the visible trait (phenotype) associated with that gene.

questions.question: State and explain the law of segregation of Mendel's.
questions.answer: Mendel's Law of Segregation states that each individual possesses two factors (alleles) for a given trait, one inherited from each parent; during the formation of gametes (meiosis), these two alleles separate (segregate) from each other, so that each gamete carries only one allele for that trait. When fertilization occurs, the offspring receives one allele from each parent, restoring the paired condition. For example, in a monohybrid cross between a pure tall pea plant (TT) and a pure short pea plant (tt), each parent produces gametes carrying only one allele (T or t). The F1 offspring are all Tt (tall, since T is dominant). When F1 plants self-pollinate, their gametes again segregate the T and t alleles, and combining randomly in fertilization produces an F2 generation in the ratio of 3 tall : 1 short (genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt), demonstrating that the alleles remain distinct and segregate independently at each generation rather than blending.

questions.question: Explain the inheritance of dihybrid cross by law.
questions.answer: A dihybrid cross studies the inheritance of two traits simultaneously and illustrates Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment, which states that alleles of different genes (controlling different traits) segregate independently of one another during gamete formation, provided the genes are located on different chromosomes (or far apart on the same chromosome). For example, crossing a pea plant that is pure for round, yellow seeds (RRYY) with one that is pure for wrinkled, green seeds (rryy) produces an F1 generation that is all RrYy (round, yellow, since round and yellow are dominant). When F1 plants (RrYy) are self-pollinated, each parent produces four types of gametes (RY, Ry, rY, ry) in equal proportion, because the segregation of the R/r pair is independent of the segregation of the Y/y pair. Combining these gametes (using a Punnett square) gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of 9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green, showing that the two traits are inherited independently of each other and can recombine in new combinations not seen in the parents.

questions.question: Explain Darwin's theory of natural selection.
questions.answer: Charles Darwin proposed the theory of natural selection (often summarised as 'survival of the fittest') as the mechanism driving evolution. It is based on several key observations and inferences: (1) Overproduction — organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support. (2) Struggle for existence — because resources (food, space, mates) are limited, offspring must compete with one another and with other species to survive. (3) Variation — individuals within a species show natural variation in their traits, some of which are heritable. (4) Survival of the fittest — individuals whose variations make them better suited to their environment are more likely to survive this struggle and reproduce successfully, while less well-adapted individuals are less likely to survive and reproduce. (5) Inheritance — favourable traits that helped an organism survive and reproduce are passed on to its offspring. Over many generations, this process causes advantageous traits to become more common in a population, gradually changing the characteristics of the species and potentially leading to the formation of new species — this is the process of evolution by natural selection.

questions.question: The life sustaining envelope of earth is:
questions.explanation: The biosphere is the thin zone of the Earth (land, water, and air) that supports and sustains life.

questions.question: The group of organisms belonging to the same species living in a particular area is called:
questions.explanation: A population consists of all individuals of the same species living together in a particular area at a given time.

questions.question: An area where community interacts with the non-living environment is called:
questions.explanation: An ecosystem is the functional unit formed by the interaction between a biological community (living organisms) and its non-living (abiotic) environment.

questions.question: Any biological region recognized by its climate or vegetation is called:
questions.explanation: A biome is a large geographic region characterized by a specific climate and the type of vegetation/organisms adapted to it (e.g., desert, forest, grassland).

questions.question: The transfer of food material from producers through some organisms with repeated eating and being eaten is called:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Food pyramid     (b) Food chain     (c) Food web     (d) Ecological pyramid
questions.explanation: A food chain describes the linear sequence of organisms through which food energy passes, from producers through successive levels of consumers.

questions.question: The elements in an ecosystem that recycle through organisms and the environment are called:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Food chain     (b) Food web     (c) Chemical cycle     (d) Biogeochemical cycle
questions.explanation: Biogeochemical cycles describe the continuous circulation of essential elements (like carbon, nitrogen) between living organisms and the physical environment.

questions.question: Process where nitrogenous compounds of living organisms convert into nitrates is called:
questions.explanation: Nitrification is the process by which ammonia/ammonium (from decomposed organic matter) is converted by bacteria into nitrites and then nitrates.

questions.question: The cold war between organisms of a community occupying the same habitat is called:
questions.explanation: Competition occurs when organisms of the same or different species vie for the same limited resources (food, space, mates) in a habitat.

questions.question: The association between two different types of organisms which get benefit from each other and cannot live without each other is called:
questions.explanation: Mutualism is a symbiotic relationship in which both interacting species benefit, and in obligate mutualism, they may be entirely dependent on each other for survival.

questions.question: The amount of solid waste or concentration of gases other than oxygen increasing in the atmosphere is called:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Air pollution     (b) Ozone depletion     (c) Acid rain     (d) Greenhouse effect
questions.explanation: Air pollution refers to the contamination of the atmosphere by harmful gases, particulates, or solid waste, degrading air quality.

questions.question: What is the effect of light on ecosystem?
questions.answer: Light is the primary source of energy for an ecosystem, as it drives photosynthesis in green plants (producers), which converts light energy into chemical energy that flows through the food chain. Light also influences the daily and seasonal activity patterns of organisms (e.g., flowering time, migration, and behaviour such as stomatal opening) and affects the distribution and diversity of species in different habitats (e.g., forest floor vs. canopy).

questions.question: Which one is the first trophic level of an ecosystem and how?
questions.answer: Producers (green plants and other photosynthetic organisms) form the first trophic level of an ecosystem because they are autotrophs that manufacture their own food using light energy through photosynthesis; they form the base of the food chain, and all other trophic levels (consumers) directly or indirectly depend on them for energy.

questions.question: What do we mean by nitrogen fixation and how does it occur in an ecosystem?
questions.answer: Nitrogen fixation is the process by which atmospheric nitrogen gas (N2), which most organisms cannot use directly, is converted into usable nitrogen compounds such as ammonia/ammonium, which plants can absorb and incorporate into proteins. It occurs mainly through nitrogen-fixing bacteria (e.g., Rhizobium living in root nodules of leguminous plants, and free-living soil bacteria like Azotobacter), as well as to a lesser extent through lightning and industrial (synthetic fertilizer) processes.

questions.question: What is interaction?
questions.answer: Interaction refers to the relationships and influences that organisms in an ecosystem have on one another and on their non-living environment, such as competition, predation, parasitism, mutualism, and commensalism, which together help maintain the balance and functioning of the ecosystem.

questions.question: What is pyramid of number?
questions.answer: A pyramid of number is a graphical representation showing the number of individual organisms present at each trophic level of a food chain, typically decreasing from producers at the base to top carnivores at the apex, illustrating how the number of organisms generally declines as energy is transferred up the food chain.

questions.question: What is greenhouse effect?
questions.answer: The greenhouse effect is the natural process by which certain atmospheric gases (greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapour) trap heat radiated from the Earth's surface, warming the planet; excessive accumulation of these gases due to human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation) intensifies this effect, causing global warming and climate change.

questions.question: What is algal bloom and how does it destroy the life of an aquatic ecosystem?
questions.answer: Algal bloom is the rapid, excessive growth of algae in a body of water, usually caused by an increase in nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen (from fertilizers, sewage, or detergents) entering the water, a process called eutrophication. This dense algal growth blocks sunlight from reaching underwater plants, and when the algae eventually die and decompose, decomposer bacteria consume large amounts of dissolved oxygen in the water, leading to oxygen depletion that suffocates fish and other aquatic organisms, disrupting the aquatic ecosystem.

questions.question: What measures can be taken to control water pollution?
questions.answer: Water pollution can be controlled by: treating industrial and domestic sewage before releasing it into water bodies; reducing and properly managing the use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides in agriculture to prevent runoff; banning/regulating the dumping of solid waste and toxic chemicals into rivers, lakes, and seas; promoting recycling and proper waste disposal; raising public awareness about water conservation and pollution; and enforcing environmental laws and regular monitoring of water quality.

questions.question: Write down the names of some endangered mammals of Pakistan.
questions.answer: Some endangered mammals of Pakistan include the Snow Leopard, Indus River Dolphin (Blind Dolphin), Markhor, Marco Polo Sheep, Chiltan Markhor, and Asiatic Black Bear.

questions.question: Draw the diagram of nitrogen cycle.
