questions.question: Describe natural asexual reproduction in plants.
questions.answer: Natural asexual (vegetative) reproduction in plants occurs without the fusion of gametes, producing offspring identical to the parent, through modified plant parts such as: Roots — e.g., sweet potato roots can develop buds that grow into new plants. Stems — e.g., runners/stolons (mint, strawberry) that creep along the ground and root at nodes; rhizomes (ginger) that are underground stems producing new shoots; tubers (potato) with 'eyes' (buds) that sprout into new plants; bulbs (onion) with fleshy, food-storing leaf bases that can grow into new plants; and suckers (banana) arising from the base of the parent stem. Leaves — e.g., in Bryophyllum, buds along the leaf margin develop into new plantlets. This form of reproduction allows plants to multiply quickly and colonize an area without depending on pollination or seed formation.

questions.question: What is pollination? Give adaptive characters of wind and insect pollinated flowers.
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther (male part) of a flower to the stigma (female part) of the same or another flower, which is a necessary step before fertilization can occur. Wind-pollinated flowers typically have: small, dull-coloured petals (or no petals) since they don't need to attract insects; no nectar or scent; large amounts of light, smooth, dry pollen produced in huge quantities to compensate for pollen wasted in air; long, feathery or exposed stigmas to catch airborne pollen; and anthers often hanging loosely outside the flower to release pollen easily into air currents. Insect-pollinated flowers typically have: large, brightly coloured petals to attract insects; scent and nectar as a reward for pollinators; pollen grains that are often sticky or spiny so they cling to an insect's body; and a sticky stigma to trap pollen brought by visiting insects.

questions.question: Describe different types of asexual reproduction in animals.
questions.answer: Asexual reproduction in animals occurs by: Binary fission — a single parent organism (e.g., Amoeba, Paramecium) divides into two equal daughter individuals. Budding — a small outgrowth (bud) forms on the parent's body (e.g., Hydra), grows, and eventually detaches to become an independent new organism, or in some cases remains attached forming a colony. Fragmentation — the parent body breaks into fragments (e.g., Planaria, starfish), and each fragment is capable of regenerating into a complete new organism. Regeneration — closely related to fragmentation, where a lost or separated body part regrows into a new complete organism in simple animals with high regenerative capacity.

questions.question: Describe the process of spermatogenesis.
questions.answer: Spermatogenesis is the process of sperm formation that occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testes. It begins with diploid germinal cells called spermatogonia, which multiply by mitosis. Some spermatogonia grow in size to become primary spermatocytes (still diploid). Each primary spermatocyte undergoes the first meiotic division to form two haploid secondary spermatocytes. Each secondary spermatocyte then undergoes the second meiotic division, producing a total of four haploid spermatids from each primary spermatocyte. These spermatids then undergo a process called spermiogenesis, in which they differentiate — developing a head (with a nucleus and acrosome containing enzymes), a middle piece (packed with mitochondria for energy), and a tail (flagellum for motility) — transforming into mature, motile sperm cells capable of fertilizing an egg.

questions.question: What is germination? Give the conditions of germination and also describe the methods of different germination.
questions.answer: Germination is the process by which a dormant seed resumes growth and develops into a seedling under favourable conditions. Conditions required for germination include: adequate water/moisture (to soften the seed coat and activate enzymes), suitable temperature (for enzyme activity and metabolic processes), sufficient oxygen (for aerobic respiration to provide energy), and in some seeds, light (though many germinate in darkness, some require light or darkness specifically). Types of germination: Epigeal germination — the hypocotyl (region below the cotyledons) elongates rapidly, pushing the cotyledons above the soil surface where they may become green and photosynthesize temporarily (e.g., bean, castor, gram). Hypogeal germination — the hypocotyl remains short, so the cotyledons stay below the soil surface, while the epicotyl (region above the cotyledons) elongates, pushing the plumule (young shoot) up through the soil (e.g., pea, maize, gram in some cases).

questions.question: Branch of biology that deals with the study of heredity and variation is called:
questions.explanation: Genetics is the specific branch of biology devoted to studying heredity (how traits pass from parents to offspring) and variation among organisms.

questions.question: The way by which genes transmit characters from parents to offspring is:
questions.explanation: Inheritance refers to the actual transmission/passing of genetic characters from parents to offspring.

questions.question: Two similar chromosomes in a cell which are similar in shape, size and position of centromere are called:
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes are pairs (one from each parent) that match in size, shape, and centromere position, carrying genes for the same traits.

questions.question: The chemical material of a chromosome is called:
questions.explanation: Chromatin is the complex of DNA and proteins that makes up the chemical material of chromosomes.

questions.question: The outer part of the DNA helix made up of sugar and phosphate is called:
questions.explanation: The sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA is held together by phosphoester (phosphodiester) bonds, forming the outer 'rails' of the double helix.

questions.question: What is a gene and how does it work?
questions.answer: A gene is a segment of DNA located on a chromosome that carries the coded instructions (in the sequence of its bases) for producing a specific protein or determining a particular trait. It works by being transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA), which is then translated at ribosomes into a specific protein; this protein then performs a function in the cell that ultimately produces the observable trait.

questions.question: Define the following terms: (a) Homologous Chromosome (b) Heterologous Chromosome (c) Dominant allele (d) Allele (e) Recessive allele (f) Homozygous (g) Heterozygous
questions.answer: (a) Homologous Chromosome: A pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, matching in size, shape, and centromere position, carrying genes for the same traits at corresponding loci. (b) Heterologous Chromosome: Chromosomes that are not matching/paired — i.e., non-homologous chromosomes that differ in size, shape, and gene content. (c) Dominant allele: An allele that expresses its effect (phenotype) whenever present, even in the presence of a different (recessive) allele, masking the recessive allele's effect. (d) Allele: One of two or more alternative forms of a gene that occupy the same position (locus) on homologous chromosomes and control the same trait. (e) Recessive allele: An allele whose effect is masked/not expressed in the phenotype when a dominant allele is present; it is only expressed when present in the homozygous condition. (f) Homozygous: Having two identical alleles (both dominant or both recessive) for a particular gene. (g) Heterozygous: Having two different alleles (one dominant, one recessive) for a particular gene.

questions.question: Which of the phenomena of inheritance is there where both factors express in heterozygous condition?
questions.answer: This phenomenon is called co-dominance (closely related to incomplete dominance), in which both alleles of a gene are fully and simultaneously expressed in the heterozygous condition, rather than one masking the other or blending — for example, in the AB blood group where both A and B alleles are expressed together.

questions.question: List out the factors which are involved in the theory of natural selection.
questions.answer: The main factors involved in Darwin's theory of natural selection are: overproduction of offspring (organisms produce more offspring than can survive); variation among individuals of a species; struggle for existence/competition for limited resources (food, space, mates); survival of the fittest (individuals with favourable variations are more likely to survive and reproduce); and inheritance of favourable variations to the next generation, gradually leading to evolutionary change over many generations.

questions.question: Relate artificial selection with natural selection.
questions.answer: In natural selection, nature/the environment acts as the selective force, allowing organisms best adapted to their environment to survive and reproduce, passing on favourable traits over many generations without human intervention. In artificial selection, humans (breeders) deliberately choose organisms with desirable traits (e.g., higher milk yield, disease resistance) to breed, intentionally guiding which traits are passed on. Both processes work on the same underlying principle — selecting individuals with particular heritable variations to reproduce more, gradually changing the characteristics of a population over generations — but natural selection is driven by environmental pressures, while artificial selection is driven by human choice.

questions.question: The small segment of DNA which has information to code one protein is called:
questions.explanation: A gene is the basic functional unit of heredity — a segment of DNA that carries the code for a specific protein or trait.

questions.question: The exact duplication of DNA is called:
questions.explanation: DNA replication is the process by which a DNA molecule makes an identical copy of itself before cell division.

questions.question: If both the parents donate the same factor(s) of a character, it is called:
questions.explanation: Homozygous refers to an individual having two identical alleles (from both parents) for a particular gene/trait.

questions.question: The genetic constitution of a trait is called:
questions.explanation: Genotype refers to the actual genetic makeup (allele combination) of an organism for a trait, as opposed to phenotype, which is its physical/observable expression.

questions.question: Describe the Watson and Crick model of DNA.
questions.answer: In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix model of DNA structure. According to this model, DNA consists of two long polynucleotide chains (strands) that are twisted around each other to form a double helix, resembling a twisted ladder. Each strand is made of a sugar (deoxyribose)-phosphate backbone on the outside, forming the 'side rails' of the ladder, connected by phosphoester bonds. The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between pairs of nitrogenous bases projecting inward, forming the 'rungs' of the ladder: Adenine (A) always pairs with Thymine (T) via two hydrogen bonds, and Guanine (G) always pairs with Cytosine (C) via three hydrogen bonds — this is called complementary base pairing. The two strands run in opposite (antiparallel) directions. This structure explained how DNA can store genetic information in the sequence of its bases and how it can be accurately copied (replicated), since each strand can serve as a template for making a new complementary strand.

questions.question: How does gene expression work? Describe in detail.
questions.answer: Gene expression is the process by which the information encoded in a gene (DNA) is used to produce a functional product, usually a protein, through two main steps: Transcription — the DNA double helix unwinds at the gene's location, and one strand acts as a template; the enzyme RNA polymerase reads this template strand and synthesizes a complementary single strand of messenger RNA (mRNA), copying the genetic code from DNA (with uracil replacing thymine). Translation — the mRNA moves from the nucleus to a ribosome in the cytoplasm, where it is 'read' three bases (a codon) at a time; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules bring specific amino acids that match each codon (via their anticodon), and the ribosome links these amino acids together in the correct sequence, forming a polypeptide chain. This polypeptide then folds into a functional protein, which carries out a specific role in the cell, ultimately producing the visible trait (phenotype) associated with that gene.

questions.question: State and explain the law of segregation of Mendel's.
questions.answer: Mendel's Law of Segregation states that each individual possesses two factors (alleles) for a given trait, one inherited from each parent; during the formation of gametes (meiosis), these two alleles separate (segregate) from each other, so that each gamete carries only one allele for that trait. When fertilization occurs, the offspring receives one allele from each parent, restoring the paired condition. For example, in a monohybrid cross between a pure tall pea plant (TT) and a pure short pea plant (tt), each parent produces gametes carrying only one allele (T or t). The F1 offspring are all Tt (tall, since T is dominant). When F1 plants self-pollinate, their gametes again segregate the T and t alleles, and combining randomly in fertilization produces an F2 generation in the ratio of 3 tall : 1 short (genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt), demonstrating that the alleles remain distinct and segregate independently at each generation rather than blending.

questions.question: Explain the inheritance of dihybrid cross by law.
questions.answer: A dihybrid cross studies the inheritance of two traits simultaneously and illustrates Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment, which states that alleles of different genes (controlling different traits) segregate independently of one another during gamete formation, provided the genes are located on different chromosomes (or far apart on the same chromosome). For example, crossing a pea plant that is pure for round, yellow seeds (RRYY) with one that is pure for wrinkled, green seeds (rryy) produces an F1 generation that is all RrYy (round, yellow, since round and yellow are dominant). When F1 plants (RrYy) are self-pollinated, each parent produces four types of gametes (RY, Ry, rY, ry) in equal proportion, because the segregation of the R/r pair is independent of the segregation of the Y/y pair. Combining these gametes (using a Punnett square) gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of 9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green, showing that the two traits are inherited independently of each other and can recombine in new combinations not seen in the parents.

questions.question: Explain Darwin's theory of natural selection.
questions.answer: Charles Darwin proposed the theory of natural selection (often summarised as 'survival of the fittest') as the mechanism driving evolution. It is based on several key observations and inferences: (1) Overproduction — organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support. (2) Struggle for existence — because resources (food, space, mates) are limited, offspring must compete with one another and with other species to survive. (3) Variation — individuals within a species show natural variation in their traits, some of which are heritable. (4) Survival of the fittest — individuals whose variations make them better suited to their environment are more likely to survive this struggle and reproduce successfully, while less well-adapted individuals are less likely to survive and reproduce. (5) Inheritance — favourable traits that helped an organism survive and reproduce are passed on to its offspring. Over many generations, this process causes advantageous traits to become more common in a population, gradually changing the characteristics of the species and potentially leading to the formation of new species — this is the process of evolution by natural selection.

questions.question: The life sustaining envelope of earth is:
questions.explanation: The biosphere is the thin zone of the Earth (land, water, and air) that supports and sustains life.

questions.question: The group of organisms belonging to the same species living in a particular area is called:
questions.explanation: A population consists of all individuals of the same species living together in a particular area at a given time.

questions.question: An area where community interacts with the non-living environment is called:
questions.explanation: An ecosystem is the functional unit formed by the interaction between a biological community (living organisms) and its non-living (abiotic) environment.

questions.question: Any biological region recognized by its climate or vegetation is called:
questions.explanation: A biome is a large geographic region characterized by a specific climate and the type of vegetation/organisms adapted to it (e.g., desert, forest, grassland).

questions.question: The transfer of food material from producers through some organisms with repeated eating and being eaten is called:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Food pyramid     (b) Food chain     (c) Food web     (d) Ecological pyramid
questions.explanation: A food chain describes the linear sequence of organisms through which food energy passes, from producers through successive levels of consumers.

questions.question: The elements in an ecosystem that recycle through organisms and the environment are called:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Food chain     (b) Food web     (c) Chemical cycle     (d) Biogeochemical cycle
questions.explanation: Biogeochemical cycles describe the continuous circulation of essential elements (like carbon, nitrogen) between living organisms and the physical environment.

questions.question: Process where nitrogenous compounds of living organisms convert into nitrates is called:
questions.explanation: Nitrification is the process by which ammonia/ammonium (from decomposed organic matter) is converted by bacteria into nitrites and then nitrates.

questions.question: The cold war between organisms of a community occupying the same habitat is called:
questions.explanation: Competition occurs when organisms of the same or different species vie for the same limited resources (food, space, mates) in a habitat.

questions.question: The association between two different types of organisms which get benefit from each other and cannot live without each other is called:
questions.explanation: Mutualism is a symbiotic relationship in which both interacting species benefit, and in obligate mutualism, they may be entirely dependent on each other for survival.

questions.question: The amount of solid waste or concentration of gases other than oxygen increasing in the atmosphere is called:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Air pollution     (b) Ozone depletion     (c) Acid rain     (d) Greenhouse effect
questions.explanation: Air pollution refers to the contamination of the atmosphere by harmful gases, particulates, or solid waste, degrading air quality.

questions.question: What is the effect of light on ecosystem?
questions.answer: Light is the primary source of energy for an ecosystem, as it drives photosynthesis in green plants (producers), which converts light energy into chemical energy that flows through the food chain. Light also influences the daily and seasonal activity patterns of organisms (e.g., flowering time, migration, and behaviour such as stomatal opening) and affects the distribution and diversity of species in different habitats (e.g., forest floor vs. canopy).

questions.question: Which one is the first trophic level of an ecosystem and how?
questions.answer: Producers (green plants and other photosynthetic organisms) form the first trophic level of an ecosystem because they are autotrophs that manufacture their own food using light energy through photosynthesis; they form the base of the food chain, and all other trophic levels (consumers) directly or indirectly depend on them for energy.

questions.question: What do we mean by nitrogen fixation and how does it occur in an ecosystem?
questions.answer: Nitrogen fixation is the process by which atmospheric nitrogen gas (N2), which most organisms cannot use directly, is converted into usable nitrogen compounds such as ammonia/ammonium, which plants can absorb and incorporate into proteins. It occurs mainly through nitrogen-fixing bacteria (e.g., Rhizobium living in root nodules of leguminous plants, and free-living soil bacteria like Azotobacter), as well as to a lesser extent through lightning and industrial (synthetic fertilizer) processes.

questions.question: What is interaction?
questions.answer: Interaction refers to the relationships and influences that organisms in an ecosystem have on one another and on their non-living environment, such as competition, predation, parasitism, mutualism, and commensalism, which together help maintain the balance and functioning of the ecosystem.

questions.question: What is pyramid of number?
questions.answer: A pyramid of number is a graphical representation showing the number of individual organisms present at each trophic level of a food chain, typically decreasing from producers at the base to top carnivores at the apex, illustrating how the number of organisms generally declines as energy is transferred up the food chain.

questions.question: What is greenhouse effect?
questions.answer: The greenhouse effect is the natural process by which certain atmospheric gases (greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapour) trap heat radiated from the Earth's surface, warming the planet; excessive accumulation of these gases due to human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation) intensifies this effect, causing global warming and climate change.

questions.question: What is algal bloom and how does it destroy the life of an aquatic ecosystem?
questions.answer: Algal bloom is the rapid, excessive growth of algae in a body of water, usually caused by an increase in nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen (from fertilizers, sewage, or detergents) entering the water, a process called eutrophication. This dense algal growth blocks sunlight from reaching underwater plants, and when the algae eventually die and decompose, decomposer bacteria consume large amounts of dissolved oxygen in the water, leading to oxygen depletion that suffocates fish and other aquatic organisms, disrupting the aquatic ecosystem.

questions.question: What measures can be taken to control water pollution?
questions.answer: Water pollution can be controlled by: treating industrial and domestic sewage before releasing it into water bodies; reducing and properly managing the use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides in agriculture to prevent runoff; banning/regulating the dumping of solid waste and toxic chemicals into rivers, lakes, and seas; promoting recycling and proper waste disposal; raising public awareness about water conservation and pollution; and enforcing environmental laws and regular monitoring of water quality.

questions.question: Write down the names of some endangered mammals of Pakistan.
questions.answer: Some endangered mammals of Pakistan include the Snow Leopard, Indus River Dolphin (Blind Dolphin), Markhor, Marco Polo Sheep, Chiltan Markhor, and Asiatic Black Bear.

questions.question: Draw the diagram of nitrogen cycle.
questions.answer: A nitrogen cycle diagram should show: atmospheric nitrogen (N2) being fixed into ammonia/ammonium by nitrogen-fixing bacteria (in root nodules and soil) and by lightning; ammonification of dead organic matter and waste by decomposers releasing ammonia; nitrification converting ammonia to nitrites and then nitrates by nitrifying bacteria; absorption of nitrates by plant roots and incorporation into proteins, which pass through the food chain to animals; and denitrification, where denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back into atmospheric nitrogen gas, completing the cycle — with arrows showing the flow between atmosphere, soil, plants, animals, and decomposers.

questions.question: Describe biotic factors of an ecosystem.
questions.answer: Biotic factors are the living components of an ecosystem, which interact with each other and with the physical environment. They are broadly classified into: Producers (autotrophs) — green plants, algae, and some bacteria that manufacture their own food through photosynthesis, forming the energy base of the ecosystem. Consumers (heterotrophs) — organisms that obtain energy by feeding on other organisms; these include primary consumers/herbivores (feeding directly on producers), secondary consumers/carnivores (feeding on herbivores), tertiary consumers/top carnivores (feeding on other carnivores), and omnivores (feeding on both plants and animals). Decomposers — bacteria and fungi that break down dead organic matter (remains of plants and animals) into simpler substances, releasing nutrients back into the soil/environment for reuse by producers, thereby recycling matter within the ecosystem. Together, these biotic components interact through relationships such as competition, predation, parasitism and mutualism, forming interconnected food chains and food webs that maintain the flow of energy and cycling of nutrients within the ecosystem.

questions.question: Describe nitrogen cycle as a biogeochemical cycle in detail.
questions.answer: The nitrogen cycle is the biogeochemical cycle by which nitrogen is converted between its various chemical forms as it circulates among the atmosphere, soil, and living organisms. Although nitrogen gas (N2) makes up about 78% of the atmosphere, most organisms cannot use it directly in this form. The cycle proceeds through several steps: (1) Nitrogen fixation — atmospheric N2 is converted into ammonia (NH3) by nitrogen-fixing bacteria (e.g., Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes, and free-living soil bacteria such as Azotobacter), and to a smaller extent by lightning and industrial fertilizer production. (2) Ammonification — decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down nitrogen-containing compounds in dead organisms and waste products, releasing ammonia/ammonium into the soil. (3) Nitrification — nitrifying bacteria (e.g., Nitrosomonas) convert ammonium into nitrites, and other bacteria (e.g., Nitrobacter) further convert nitrites into nitrates, a form readily absorbed by plant roots. (4) Assimilation — plants absorb nitrates and incorporate nitrogen into organic molecules such as amino acids and proteins; animals then obtain nitrogen by consuming plants or other animals. (5) Denitrification — under anaerobic conditions, denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which is released into the atmosphere, completing the cycle. This continuous cycling ensures that nitrogen, essential for making proteins and nucleic acids, remains available to sustain life.

questions.question: What is pollution? Describe different types of hazardous effects caused by air pollution.
questions.answer: Pollution is the introduction of harmful substances or contaminants into the environment (air, water, or soil) that cause adverse changes, making the environment unsafe or unsuitable for living organisms. Air pollution — contamination of air by harmful gases (e.g., carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides), smoke, dust, and particulate matter, mainly from vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, and burning of fossil fuels — causes several hazardous effects: it contributes to respiratory diseases in humans such as asthma, bronchitis, and lung cancer; it causes acid rain, when sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides react with atmospheric moisture to form acidic precipitation that damages crops, forests, buildings, and aquatic ecosystems; it leads to depletion of the ozone layer (due to chlorofluorocarbons), which normally protects Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation, increasing risks of skin cancer and eye damage; and it enhances the greenhouse effect, trapping excess heat in the atmosphere and contributing to global warming and climate change, which disrupts ecosystems and weather patterns worldwide.

questions.question: The artificial manipulation, medication and recombination of DNA is:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Genetic engineering     (b) Biotechnology     (c) Molecular biology     (d) Genetic
questions.explanation: Genetic engineering specifically refers to the direct, artificial manipulation and recombination of an organism's DNA.

questions.question: The earlier biotechnologists were:
questions.explanation: Long before modern science, farmers were the earliest 'biotechnologists,' using selective breeding and fermentation techniques without understanding the underlying genetics.

questions.question: The complete graph (map) of the human genome was studied by:
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project (HGP) was the international scientific effort that mapped and sequenced the entire human genome.

questions.question: Alcohol and antibiotics on a large scale production by organism is an area of:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Environmental biotechnology     (b) Fermentation     (c) Biotechnology in industry     (d) Medicinal biotechnology
questions.explanation: Large-scale industrial production of substances like alcohol and antibiotics using microorganisms falls under industrial/biotechnology in industry.

questions.question: Most of the living things use O2 to produce:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) ATP     (b) Alcohol     (c) Organic acid     (d) Ecological pyramid
questions.explanation: Most organisms use oxygen in aerobic respiration to efficiently produce ATP, the cell's energy currency.

questions.question: In acidic formulation, lactic acid is produced from:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Pyruvic acid     (b) Acetic acid     (c) Citric acid     (d) Glyceric acid
questions.explanation: In lactic acid fermentation, pyruvic acid (produced from glucose breakdown) is reduced to form lactic acid in the absence of oxygen.

questions.question: The bread dough rises during alcoholic fermentation due to:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Methyl alcohol     (b) CO2     (c) Ethyl alcohol     (d) H2O
questions.explanation: Yeast performs alcoholic fermentation on sugars in dough, releasing carbon dioxide gas, whose bubbles cause the dough to rise.

questions.question: The container used to grow bacteria on a large scale is called:
questions.explanation: Fermenters (bioreactors) are large vessels designed to provide optimal, controlled conditions for growing microorganisms on an industrial scale.

questions.question: The naturally occurring enzyme used as a defense chemical by bacteria is:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Defense protein     (b) Restriction enzyme     (c) Hydrolytic enzyme     (d) ligase enzyme
questions.explanation: Restriction enzymes naturally occur in bacteria as a defense mechanism, cutting up foreign (e.g., viral) DNA that invades the cell.

questions.question: Extra circular DNA which is used as a vector of genes is:
questions.explanation: Plasmids are small, circular pieces of extra-chromosomal DNA found in bacteria, commonly used as vectors to carry and transfer genes in genetic engineering.

questions.question: What kind of enzymes allow scientists to cut and paste pieces of DNA together to form recombinant DNA?
questions.answer: Restriction enzymes are used to 'cut' DNA at specific recognition sequences, and DNA ligase is used to 'paste' (join) DNA fragments together, allowing scientists to combine DNA from different sources to form recombinant DNA.

questions.question: Explain how making human tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells is an example of genetic engineering.
questions.answer: In this process, the human gene coding for tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA), a protein that helps dissolve blood clots, is isolated and inserted into Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells using genetic engineering techniques. Since the human gene has been artificially introduced into a different (animal) cell type, and the CHO cells then use this foreign gene's instructions to manufacture the human t-PA protein on a large scale, this is a clear example of genetic engineering — producing a specific, useful protein by transferring and expressing a gene from one organism in another.

questions.question: How do organisms obtain energy? How does fermentation work?
questions.answer: Organisms obtain energy mainly by breaking down food molecules (like glucose) through cellular respiration, releasing chemical energy stored in their bonds and converting it into a usable form, ATP. When oxygen is available, this occurs through aerobic respiration, which yields a large amount of ATP. Fermentation is an anaerobic (without oxygen) pathway used by some organisms/cells when oxygen is limited: glucose is partially broken down (through glycolysis) to pyruvic acid, which is then converted into end-products such as lactic acid (lactic acid fermentation, e.g., in muscles and some bacteria) or ethanol and carbon dioxide (alcoholic fermentation, e.g., in yeast), regenerating a molecule (NAD+) needed to keep glycolysis running and producing a small amount of ATP.

questions.question: What types of microorganisms cause fermentation to occur?
questions.answer: Fermentation is mainly caused by yeasts (fungi, e.g., Saccharomyces, responsible for alcoholic fermentation in bread and brewing) and certain bacteria (e.g., Lactobacillus and Streptococcus species, responsible for lactic acid fermentation in yogurt and cheese production).

questions.question: What food and non-food products are created by fermentation?
questions.answer: Food products created by fermentation include: yogurt and cheese (from milk, using lactic acid bacteria), bread (using yeast for alcoholic fermentation, producing CO2 to raise dough), pickles and sauerkraut (using lactic acid bacteria on vegetables), and alcoholic beverages such as beer and wine (using yeast). Non-food products include industrially produced alcohol (ethanol) for fuel or solvents, and antibiotics and other pharmaceuticals produced through microbial fermentation.

questions.question: What are some advantages and disadvantages of fermentation in food processing?
questions.answer: Advantages: fermentation acts as a natural preservative, allowing fermented foods to last longer; it can enhance flavour, texture, and nutritional value of foods; and it is a relatively low-cost, low-energy method of food production and processing. Disadvantages: fermentation can be difficult to control precisely, and contamination by unwanted microorganisms can spoil the product or make it unsafe; the process can be slow compared to other preservation methods; and some fermented products may not appeal to all consumers due to their distinct taste, smell, or texture.

questions.question: What factors can affect the fermentation process?
questions.answer: Fermentation can be affected by factors such as temperature (each microorganism has an optimal temperature range for enzyme activity), pH of the medium, availability and concentration of nutrients/substrate (e.g., sugar), oxygen levels (since fermentation is typically anaerobic, excess oxygen can inhibit it or shift metabolism), the type and amount of microorganism (starter culture) used, and the presence of any contaminating or competing microorganisms.

questions.question: Define biotechnology.
questions.answer: Biotechnology can be defined as the use of living organisms, biological systems, or their cellular components to develop or produce useful products or processes for the benefit of humankind, including precise genetic improvement of living things.

questions.question: What is classical biotechnology?
questions.answer: Classical biotechnology refers to the traditional, older applications of biotechnology that were used before modern genetic engineering techniques were developed, such as using microorganisms for fermentation (bread-making, brewing, cheese and yogurt production), and traditional selective breeding of plants and animals to improve desired traits.

questions.question: What is your justification in considering biotechnology as an old technology?
questions.answer: Biotechnology can be considered an old technology because humans have been using living organisms and biological processes for thousands of years — for example, ancient civilizations used yeast for fermenting bread and alcoholic beverages, used bacteria to make cheese and yogurt, and practiced selective breeding of crops and livestock to enhance desirable traits — long before the modern scientific understanding of genetics, DNA, and genetic engineering existed.

questions.question: Describe the contribution of Louis Pasteur toward the development of classical biotechnology.
questions.answer: Louis Pasteur made major contributions to biotechnology by discovering that fermentation is caused by living microorganisms (yeast and bacteria), disproving the theory of spontaneous generation. He developed pasteurization, a heat-treatment process that kills harmful microorganisms in liquids like milk and wine without significantly altering their quality, which greatly improved food safety and preservation. His work laid the scientific foundation for understanding and controlling microbial fermentation processes used in classical biotechnology.

questions.question: What are the different types of fermentation?
questions.answer: The two major types of (anaerobic) fermentation are: Lactic acid fermentation, in which pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid (occurs in some bacteria and in animal muscle cells during strenuous exercise), and Alcoholic (ethanol) fermentation, in which pyruvic acid is converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide (carried out by yeasts, used in baking and brewing).

questions.question: What is lactic acid bacillus? Explain its role in the formation of curd.
questions.answer: Lactic acid bacillus (e.g., Lactobacillus) is a type of bacteria that carries out lactic acid fermentation. When added to milk, it ferments the milk sugar (lactose) into lactic acid; the increasing acidity causes milk proteins (casein) to coagulate and thicken, converting liquid milk into semi-solid curd (yogurt), while also giving it its characteristic tangy taste.

questions.question: Name some of the fermented food products of Pakistan.
questions.answer: Fermented food products commonly found in Pakistan include yogurt (dahi), lassi, cheese (paneer), pickles (achar), naan/bread (leavened using yeast), and traditional fermented dairy products such as makhan (butter) and desi ghee production which involves fermentation of cream.

questions.question: Name four recombinant DNA products available on the market.
questions.answer: Four examples of recombinant DNA products available on the market are: human insulin (for diabetes treatment), human growth hormone, hepatitis B vaccine, and tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA, used to dissolve blood clots).

questions.question: Who is called the father of antiseptic?
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Alexander Fleming     (b) Edward Jenner     (c) Lister     (d) Oswald Schmiedeberg
questions.explanation: Joseph Lister is known as the father of antiseptic surgery for introducing antiseptic techniques that greatly reduced surgical infections.

questions.question: Drugs for treatment of rheumatoid arthritis can be obtained from:
questions.explanation: Many anti-inflammatory drugs used for conditions like rheumatoid arthritis are derived from plant sources (e.g., compounds related to salicin from willow bark).

questions.question: Drugs that slow normal brain functioning are categorized as:
questions.explanation: Sedatives are drugs that depress/slow down central nervous system activity, calming brain function.

questions.question: Vaccination can be administered:
questions.optionsRaw: (a) After infection     (b) Before infection     (c) During infection     (d) All are Correct
questions.explanation: Vaccines are typically given before exposure to a disease, to build immunity in advance so the body can respond quickly if it encounters the actual pathogen later.

questions.question: The substance which inhibits the growth of bacteria can be considered as:
questions.explanation: A bacteriostatic substance stops or slows the growth/multiplication of bacteria without necessarily killing them (unlike bactericidal agents, which kill bacteria).

questions.question: Haris is addicted to a drug, which left the following effects on Haris: (i) Blurred vision (ii) Making unseen faces in imagination (iii) Euphoria. Identify the drug to which Haris is addicted.
questions.explanation: Hallucinogens cause perceptual disturbances such as seeing things that aren't there (hallucinations), blurred vision, and euphoria, matching the described symptoms.

questions.question: Which one is not the effect of misuse of antibiotics?
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Diarrhea     (b) Immunization     (c) Stomach upset     (d) Antibiotic resistance
questions.explanation: Immunization is a deliberate, beneficial medical process (unrelated to antibiotic misuse), whereas diarrhea, stomach upset, and antibiotic resistance are all known harmful side effects of antibiotic misuse.

questions.question: Why are antibiotics not effective against viral infections?
questions.answer: Antibiotics work by targeting specific structures or processes found in bacterial cells, such as bacterial cell walls, ribosomes, or metabolic pathways, which are absent in viruses. Since viruses are not independent cells (they lack their own cell wall, ribosomes, and metabolism, and instead hijack the host's cellular machinery to replicate), antibiotics have no target to act upon in viruses, making them ineffective against viral infections.

questions.question: Why are sedatives used for?
questions.answer: Sedatives are used to calm the central nervous system, reducing anxiety, agitation, or excitement; they are often prescribed to promote relaxation, relieve insomnia (aid sleep), and to help patients remain calm before certain medical or surgical procedures.

questions.question: Why is addiction considered a harmful condition?
questions.answer: Addiction is considered harmful because it involves a compulsive, uncontrollable craving and use of a substance despite negative consequences; it can cause physical dependence (withdrawal symptoms when the drug is stopped), damage to organs (e.g., liver, brain, heart), impaired mental and physical health, disruption of personal relationships and social/work life, and can lead to overdose or death.

questions.question: How can drugs (medicine) be taken from natural sources?
questions.answer: Drugs can be obtained from natural sources such as plants (e.g., quinine from cinchona bark, morphine from opium poppy, aspirin-related compounds from willow bark), animals (e.g., insulin originally extracted from pig/cow pancreas), microorganisms (e.g., antibiotics like penicillin from the fungus Penicillium), and minerals (e.g., certain mineral-based medicinal compounds).

questions.question: Is it possible to get drugs from animals? Name some of them.
questions.answer: Yes, drugs can be obtained from animals. Examples include insulin (originally extracted from the pancreas of pigs and cattle for diabetes treatment), heparin (an anticoagulant obtained from animal tissues, e.g., pig intestines), and certain hormone-based medicines and antitoxins/antivenoms produced using animal-derived antibodies.

questions.question: Do we have any harm from antibiotics? If so, mention them.
questions.answer: Yes, antibiotics can cause harm, including: side effects such as diarrhea, stomach upset, and allergic reactions; disruption of the body's normal, beneficial bacterial flora, which can lead to secondary infections (e.g., fungal infections like thrush); and, most significantly, antibiotic resistance, where bacteria evolve mechanisms to survive antibiotic treatment due to overuse or misuse, making infections harder to treat in the future.

questions.question: How does a vaccine work against a pathogen? Explain the process with the help of a diagram.
questions.answer: A vaccine contains a weakened, killed, or partial form of a pathogen (or its toxins/surface proteins) that cannot cause full-blown disease but is still recognized by the immune system as foreign. When administered, the immune system's white blood cells detect these antigens and respond by producing specific antibodies against them; some of these cells become memory cells that remain in the body long-term. If the person is later exposed to the actual live pathogen, these memory cells allow the immune system to recognize it quickly and mount a fast, strong antibody response, destroying the pathogen before it can cause disease. (A diagram should show: vaccine (antigen) injection → recognition by immune cells → antibody production and memory cell formation → rapid secondary response upon real pathogen exposure, providing immunity.)

questions.question: How do bacteria produce antibiotic resistance?
questions.answer: Bacteria develop antibiotic resistance through several mechanisms, often accelerated by overuse or misuse of antibiotics. Due to natural genetic variation, some bacteria in a population may already carry (or acquire through random mutation) genes that allow them to survive exposure to an antibiotic — for example, by producing enzymes that break down the drug, altering the drug's target site so it no longer binds effectively, pumping the antibiotic out of the cell before it can act, or changing their cell wall/membrane permeability to prevent the drug from entering. When an antibiotic is used, susceptible bacteria are killed, but any resistant bacteria survive and continue to multiply, passing their resistance genes to their offspring. Resistance genes can also spread between different bacteria (even different species) through plasmid transfer. Over time and repeated antibiotic exposure, resistant strains become dominant in the population, resulting in bacteria that the antibiotic can no longer effectively treat — a serious global health problem.

questions.question: Describe the mode of vaccination.
questions.answer: Vaccination is the process of administering a vaccine to stimulate an individual's immune system to develop protective immunity against a specific disease, without causing the disease itself. It typically works as follows: A vaccine containing a weakened/inactivated pathogen, a piece of the pathogen (e.g., a protein or toxin), or genetic material coding for a pathogen's antigen is introduced into the body, usually by injection (though some vaccines are given orally or nasally). The immune system recognizes the vaccine's antigens as foreign and responds by activating white blood cells (lymphocytes), which produce specific antibodies against the antigen and also form memory cells that persist long after vaccination. If the vaccinated person is later exposed to the actual disease-causing pathogen, these memory cells enable the immune system to recognize and respond to the pathogen much faster and more strongly than in an unvaccinated person, preventing the pathogen from establishing infection or causing severe illness. Some vaccines require multiple doses (booster shots) over time to build strong, long-lasting immunity.
